subject: JavaScript & Node.js Foundations
title: Prelim Summative Exam — Wk1–6 (Node Internals to Docker Intro)

questions.text: Which variable declaration is block-scoped and CANNOT be reassigned?
questions.hint: Think about which keyword locks the binding, not necessarily the contents.

questions.text: Which comparison operator checks BOTH value and type?
questions.hint: It's the one you should always prefer over the two-equals version.

questions.text: Which array method transforms every item and returns a NEW array?
questions.hint: This one always returns an array of the same length as the original.

questions.text: What is a closure?
options: A function that runs immediately after being defined
A function that remembers variables from where it was created, even after the outer function has finished
A method that closes a file stream
A way to stop a loop early
questions.hint: The counter() example in the cheatsheet demonstrates this.

questions.text: Where does `await` work?
questions.hint: It's a key rule stated directly in the reviewer.

questions.text: What makes Node.js able to handle many concurrent connections without spawning a thread per request?
options: Multiple V8 engines running in parallel
questions.hint: I/O is handed off and callbacks are queued to run when ready.

questions.text: Why is `path.join()` preferred over hardcoding `/` in file paths?
options: It runs faster than string concatenation
It automatically creates the folders if they don't exist
It builds paths correctly across different operating systems
It converts relative paths to URLs
questions.hint: Windows uses a different path separator than macOS/Linux.

questions.text: In semver, what does `~1.2.3` allow?
questions.hint: Compare it to the caret (^) which allows more.

questions.text: Which of these runs SOONEST among the three?
options: They all run at the same time
questions.hint: It runs even before microtasks like Promises.

questions.text: What does `process.exit(1)` signal?
questions.hint: Exit code 0 means success — anything else means what?

questions.text: Which best describes `process.on('uncaughtException', ...)`?
options: The primary way to handle all errors in production
A safety net, never a primary error-handling strategy
A method to prevent errors from ever occurring
A required part of every Node.js app
questions.hint: The reviewer explicitly warns against relying on this to 'handle' errors.

questions.text: Why do Streams matter compared to `fs.readFile`?
options: Streams are only for writing files, not reading
Streams process data in chunks, keeping memory flat regardless of file size
Streams are faster at compiling JavaScript
questions.hint: readFile loads the ENTIRE file into memory at once — streams don't.

questions.text: A client sends a request with a missing required field. Which status code fits best?
questions.hint: This is a malformed request — whose fault is that, client or server?

questions.text: Why is GET considered idempotent while POST is not?
options: GET requests are always faster than POST
Calling GET repeatedly leaves the system in the same state, while POST can create new resources each time
GET cannot be cached, but POST can
POST requests never have a body
questions.hint: Think about what happens if you run POST /users twice.

questions.text: In the Dockerfile, why is `COPY package*.json ./` placed BEFORE `COPY . .`?
options: Docker requires package.json to be copied first by rule
So npm install can run without internet access
To let Docker cache the npm install layer and speed up rebuilds when only source code changes
questions.hint: It's about Docker's layer caching behavior.

questions.text: This JavaScript variable keyword is function-scoped, hoisted, and generally advised against using in modern code.
questions.hint: It's the oldest of the three declaration keywords.

questions.text: This array method folds/reduces an entire array down into a single value.
questions.hint: Its name literally describes what it does to the array.

questions.text: This is Google's JavaScript engine that compiles JS to machine code and also powers Chrome.
questions.hint: Named after a type of car engine.

questions.text: This built-in Node.js module is used for safe, cross-platform building of file paths (e.g. joining directories and filenames).
questions.hint: Its name is also the word for the string it constructs.

questions.text: This file lists a Node.js project's metadata, scripts, and dependencies.
questions.hint: Every npm project has one at its root.

questions.text: This Node.js global object gives access to CLI arguments (argv), environment variables (env), and the current working directory (cwd).
questions.hint: It's also what you call `.exit(1)` on to signal failure.

questions.text: This core Node.js class allows objects to emit named events and register listeners for them; `http.Server` itself is one.
questions.hint: It's imported from the 'events' module.

questions.text: This type of stream both reads AND modifies data as it passes through, then writes it out (e.g., an uppercase converter).
questions.hint: It's one of the four stream types listed in the cheatsheet.

questions.text: This HTTP status code means the request succeeded but there is nothing to send back — commonly returned on a successful DELETE.
questions.hint: It's in the 2xx success range, but distinct from 200.

questions.text: This file works like `.gitignore` but excludes files (e.g. node_modules, .git, .env) from being copied into a Docker image.
questions.hint: Its name pairs the word 'ignore' with the container platform's name.
